item.title: From Mesopotamian goddesses to Victorian prudery: the history of female sexuality in 13 facts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

From Mesopotamian goddesses to Victorian prudery: the history of female sexuality in 13 facts

A nun with a superior erotic understanding, Pompeia and her bedroom circumstances, and an ongoing quest for equality. Here’s what the historical record tells us about women’s sex lives down the ages

To hear the old cliché, you’d think that for centuries before modern feminism, women simply lay back and thought of England. Or, depending on the century and the woman, of ancient Athens, the Habsburg Empire or the French Third Republic.

It’s a poor version of history. Women have always found ways to express desire, and at times their appetites have been cause for celebration. But there’s a darker history here, too, of hypocrisy and repression, and of the fear a woman who knows what she wants can inspire.

Speaking on the HistoryExtra podcast about her book, Flick: The Story of Female Pleasure, Kate Lister offers 13 takeaways from her work.

What were prehistoric phallic objects used for?

At Hohle Fels cave in south-western Germany, archaeologists recovered a polished stone phallus roughly 30,000 years old, measuring about 20 centimetres long. Fashioned from fine-grained siltstone, it was reconstructed from 14 fragments, with a piece discovered in 2004 allowing researchers to piece together earlier finds.

- Read more | From magic spells to dirty graffiti: 16 surprising facts about sex in the classical world

But while there’s no ambiguity about its shape, its function is more difficult to ascertain.

“Archaeologists find quite a lot of those. But then the question is, “well, what were they?”” asks Lister. Could women in prehistory have used objects like the Hohle Fels phallus for their own sexual pleasure? “Were they sex objects? Were they erotic objects? Were they lucky objects? We’re just not sure.”

Despite this ambiguity, the very existence of these artefacts shows that the human interest in creating representations of genitals goes back a very long way indeed.

“Clearly from our earliest ancestors, we have been very aware of phalluses and vulvas, and they have symbolically meant quite a lot to us.”

Ancient goddesses of fertility could be “quite horny”

Calling an ancient deity a “fertility goddess” instantly makes you think of crops, childbirth and motherhood. But that description certainly doesn’t do justice to the identity of the Mesopotamian goddess Inanna. “She is quite a horny, naughty goddess,” says Lister.

In Sumerian songs about Inanna and her lover Dumuzid, lovemaking and agricultural abundance were closely connected. Images of cultivating land and producing fruitful crops symbolically expressed sexual attraction and satisfaction.

“Prudish historians in the 19th century refer to her a goddess of fertility, but it’s not really fertility. There are erotic songs sung about her, and stories about her sex life that are legendary.”

Women were once portrayed as the more lustful sex

Any idea that women naturally want less sex than men would have puzzled many ancient and medieval writers. Some portrayed women as the more lustful sex, supposedly less capable of governing their appetites. In classical Athens, that stereotype appeared in popular literature alongside arguments about women’s place in society.

“For the ancient Greeks, the idea of control is incredibly important. You control your baser emotions,” Lister explains.

Self-restraint demonstrated moral strength. Describing women as sexually voracious was therefore hardly a compliment: women’s supposed lack of control could become a justification for supervising their behaviour.

The stereotype also supplied material for comedy. In Aristophanes’ Lysistrata, women propose withholding sex to force men to end a war – but some initially recoil at the prospect of abstaining themselves.

Caesar’s wife faced a sexual double standard

“The first thing that you need to know in this story is that Julius Caesar was an absolute dirt bag,” says Lister. “All of the sources tell us this about him. He has a reputation for having sex with his friends’ wives and his enemies’ wives.”

- Read more | Cleopatra, Julius Caesar and Mark Antony: how the last pharaoh's love affairs shaped Ancient Egypt's fate

But while Caesar’s sexual exploits inspired songs, his wife’s suspected involvement in a scandal ended her marriage. In 62 BC, the Roman aristocrat Publius Clodius Culcher entered a women-only religious ceremony in Caesar’s household, allegedly seeking an illicit meeting with Caesar’s wife, Pompeia.

“There’s no evidence she reciprocated his feelings, but just a hint of it is enough, and they get divorced. Poor Pompeia.”

Early Christian thinkers helped cast sexual pleasure as sinful

Saint Jerome, a priest and theologian who lived during the final centuries of the Western Roman empire, exerted an enormous intellectual influence as Christianity grew. That influence extended to perceptions of sex.

Lister identifies Jerome as one of the early Christian writers who advanced the idea that pleasure itself was sinful. Alongside suspicion of pleasure came the veneration of virginity. But this ideal presented an obvious practical difficulty.

“Saint Jerome would’ve preferred if everybody was a virgin, but obviously this presents a bit of a conundrum for the early church fathers because if everyone’s a virgin, they’re going to run out of Christians pretty quick.”

The resulting concession, as Lister characterises it, permitted sex while remaining deeply suspicious of its pleasures.

A medieval abbess wrote about female orgasm

A medieval abbess might seem an unlikely source for an account of female orgasm. But Hildegard of Bingen, the 12th-century German religious leader and writer, candidly discussed women’s sexual responses in the medical work known as Causae et curae.

“She wasn’t just a nun. She was the mother superior, and she was a polymath, and she did all kinds of amazing stuff,” says Lister.…

item.title: 5 Strange and Brutal Methods of Execution Throughout History
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Humans have experimented with a lot of different execution methods over the years, with the most commonly used these days being lethal injection, electrocution, and hanging. But in the past there were many more ways of carrying out lethal punishmentâsome of which are as strange as they are horrifying.

Historians actually now doubt that some of the most brutal methods of execution attributed to centuries past were real. For instance, the brazen bull (which involved someone being placed inside of a hollow bronze bull and then a fire being lit underneath it) and the blood eagle (cutting open a personâs back and pulling their lungs out to create wings) both fall into the likely-fictional category. But there are other gruesomely creative execution methods from history that were definitely realâincluding the five examples below.

Boiling in a Volcano

Volcanoes have caused thousands of accidental deaths throughout history, with pyroclastic flows and explosive blasts being the most common ways people are killed by them. But from the early 17th century to the early 19th century, Mount Unzen in Japan was also deliberately used to brutally execute people.

During Japanâs Edo period, the Tokugawa shogunate feared the spread of Christianity and so essentially put the country under lockdown. Any Christians who were discovered were tortured and ordered to abandon their religion, and anyone who refused was executed in a rather unusualâand very painfulâway. They would be taken to Mount Unzen, a volcano located at the western tip of Japan, and thrown into its bubbling hot springs. Although it was a fairly fast deathâno one could survive long in the acidic boiling waterâit would have been agonizing.

Death by Elephant

For hundreds of years, elephants were trained to carry out public executions in South and Southeast Asia. The huge animals would place one of their massive feet on the condemned personâs head or torso to quickly crush them to death. But there were a few otherâfar cruelerâways that elephants could carry out the death penalty. In 1850, British diplomat Henry Charles Sirr described elephants in Sri Lanka âbeing taught to prolong the agony of the wretched sufferers by crushing the limbs, avoiding the vital parts.â The huge animals could also tear a person limb from limb with the aid of their trunk, or they could cut a person to death with the aid of blades that were fitted onto their tusks or feet. The practice of execution by elephant started dying out during the 17th and 18th centuries, when European countries began colonizing South and Southeast Asia.

Keelhauling

Itâs often thought that people were executed at sea by being made to walk the plank, but this punishment was surprisingly used very rarely, and the reality was actually much worse. Some sailors were subjected to the horrors of keelhauling, which was invented by the Dutch and was used from around the mid-1600s to the mid-1800s.

A line of rope would be looped around the shipâs keel, and the victim would be tied to one end and then dropped into the sea. Those on deck would then pull the other end, dragging the poor person across the keelâwhere they would be cut and bludgeoned by barnacles, ringbolts, and chains. This process would often be repeated multiple times; according to William Falconerâs An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (1780), âit is continued till the culprit is almost suffocated for want of air, benumbed with the cold of water, or stunned with the blows his head received by striking the shipâs bottom.â Although not always intended to be fatal, in practice the punishment would often end in death.

A particularly gruesome account of keelhauling, which occurred aboard the Egyptian vessel the Mehemet Ali, was described in 1882. Two sailors were subjected to the punishment and the news correspondent aboard wrote that âthe nose of one wretch was torn almost away, one ear was gone, and the shreds of the clothing he had worn clung to him only where they were held by his bonds. He was blood literally from head to foot. His companionâs condition was equally horrible.â Both men were unconscious and the reporter assumed they were dead.Â

Schwedentrunk

During Thirty Yearsâ Warâwhich lasted from 1618 to 1648âSwedish soldiers gained a reputation for a particularly disgusting way of killing their German enemies: Schwedentrunk, which in German translates to âSwedish drink.â A funnel would be forced into the victimâs mouth and then a huge quantity of foul liquid (which was also sometimes boiling hot) was poured down their throat. Liquids used included dirty water, urine, and manure.

As you can imagine, schwedentrunk was an incredibly painful way to die, with the personâs intestines usually being filled to bursting. If they didnât burst, then bacterial infection was likely to finish the person off. âSo growing sicke, and their bellies swelling like a Tun, they have died by leysure with the greater torment,â wrote Philip Vincent in The Lamentations of Germany (1638).

The Breaking Wheel

The wheel is one of humanityâs most important inventions, but itâs not only been used for good. The breaking wheel was a torture and execution device that dates back to Ancient Rome and was still sometimes used up until the 19th century. There were a variety of ways in which the wheel could be used to kill someone. Some executioners would drop the wheel itself onto a victim to break their bones, but most often the condemned person was tied to the wheelâeither across the spokes or bent around the rim. From there they were usually beaten to death with a cudgel or hammer, and sometimes a fire was also lit beneath them.

Someone tied to the breaking wheel could be put out of their misery with just one or two blows, but some people suffered many more than that. In 1581, German serial killer Peter Niersâwho was convicted of a staggering 544 murdersâwas subjected to a deliberately prolonged death, receiving 42 blows over the course of two days.…

item.title: The First Black Friday Was Nothing Like the Shopping Frenzy We Know Today
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Black Friday hasnât always been about filling shopping bags to the brim and taking advantage of online deals.

According to History, the first Black Friday had nothing to do with clothing discounts or shoppers fighting over the latest retail items. The date wasnât even close to Thanksgiving.

So, what really happened on the first âBlack Friday,â and how did it evolve into a shopping holiday that spurs Americans to camp outside stores and relentlessly add to their online shopping carts?Â

Letâs flip back a page or two in American history and see what we can find!Â

THE FIRST BLACK FRIDAY

The first Black Friday was on September 24, 1869, otherwise known as the crash of the U.S. gold market.Â

Two devious Wall Street financiers, Jay Gould and Jim Fisk, let greed consume them and decided to buy as much gold as they could get their hands on, drive up its price, and sell it for a greater profit. This wasnât the first time the deceitful pair had resorted to such schemes. According to PBS, one year earlier, they âused stock fraud and bribery to keep Cornelius Vanderbilt from taking control of the Erie Railroad.â

Connected to President Ulysses S. Grant through his brother-in-law, Abel Rathbone Corbin, Gould and Fisk put a bug in the Commander-in-Chiefâs ear, persuading him not to sell more gold so its value would rise. With Corbinâs approval, General Daniel Butterfield became assistant treasurer of the United States and promised to keep Gould and Fisk privy to the government's gold transactions.Â

When Grant discovered what Corbin, and therefore Butterfield, was doing behind the scenes, he âordered the sale of $4,000,000 in government gold.â This decreased the price of gold from $160 to $133 and sent the stock market tumbling down. Investors immediately panicked, brokerage houses went bankrupt, and the market fell 20 percent, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Investors who had borrowed money to buy gold at the higher price suddenly couldnât repay their loans, and Corbin was among them. Gould, however, was savvy enough to sell his gold before the collapse. He ended up controlling the Union Pacific Railroad, Western Union Telegraph Company, and the Manhattan Elevated Railroad. His partner, whom he hadnât told of his sales, wasnât so lucky.

Three years after the first Black Friday, Fisk was shot and killed by financier Edward Stokes, ironically, during a dispute that involved money. Neither Gould nor Fisk ever served time behind bars for the scandal that caused the first Black Friday.

BLACK FRIDAY REIMAGINED

The term was reborn in the 1950s, when tourists traveled to Philadelphia in droves on the Friday after Thanksgiving for the annual ArmyâNavy football game. Police officers worked extra shifts to manage the crowds, according to History. Shoplifters contributed to the chaos by stealing from stores, demanding more attention from law enforcement.

From then on, Philadelphia referred to the day as âBlack Friday.â In 1961, local officials tried to rename it âBig Friday,â but it didnât catch on. Then, in the 1980s, retailersÂ reinterpreted Black Friday as a day when stores moved from red (operating at a loss) to black (making a profit) through extensive holiday discounts.Â

Though we've held on to this version of Black Friday for decades, its story began with the U.S. gold market crash of 1869 and Philadelphiaâs hectic ArmyâNavy weekend in the â50s.Â

Today, the beloved shopping holiday isnât even contained to a single day. It now spans online and in-store sales that begin weeks in advance and continue for days afterward. In 2026, we can be thankful that Black Friday has nothing to do with stock market crashes and lawless shopping chaos.

Happy shopping!Â

item.title: Ancient Romans hated Nero – and this is the surprising way they showed their disdain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Ancient Romans hated Nero – and this is the surprising way they showed their disdain

"The simple act of writing a name can also be a political statement", writes Kavita Puri

For the past 10 years, walking under the same railway bridge near my home each day, I’ve read a piece of graffiti written in black spray paint in capital letters: “BREXIT WAS SOLD TO US BY LIARS.” It has become part of the landscape, just as much as the local convenience store, pub and gym. These words are high up on the wall of the bridge – maybe too high for easy removal.

To some people, these seven words may be seen as vandalism or destruction of property. But they can also be seen as a form of public expression – even protest – in a democracy. So much of the iconography of the past – such as statues and grand buildings – signifies power and celebrates the powerful, whereas graffiti often gives voice to the ordinary people.

The word graffiti seems to have been coined in 1851 from the Italian word graffito, meaning ‘a scratch’, used by archaeologists to describe writing they found on walls in Pompeii. Because, of course, political graffiti has existed for thousands of years. Some of the earliest and best-documented examples are those words inscribed in Pompeii, from before its destruction in AD 79. During excavations, thousands of painted endorsements for political election candidates were discovered on walls. There were also insults, satire, even jokes about potential candidates and officials.

WATCH | Pompeii wasn’t destroyed when you think it was

Writings from the time also suggest that graffiti was a popular way for the people of Rome to voice their displeasure about the actions of their leaders, written on walls, columns and even placards hung around the necks of statues. Plutarch wrote that Brutus was apparently encouraged to join the conspiracy against Julius Caesar after seeing graffiti written under cover of darkness. And Suetonius wrote that, towards the end of Nero’s reign, when food prices were particularly high and the notorious emperor was increasingly unpopular, mocking graffiti around the city criticised imperial excesses.

However, only 10 per cent of ancient Romans could read. But by the 18th century, literacy rates in Paris had reached around 50 per cent. In the years before the French Revolution of 1789, the statue of King Louis XV, standing where the Place de la Concorde is today, was frequently daubed with graffiti criticising the monarchy. Things got so bad that railings had to be put around it, and soldiers were on guard night and day.

Graffiti has often been used in conflicts. In May 1945, when the Soviets took Berlin, they wrote their names and victorious slogans in the Reichstag – lettering that has been preserved in the reconstructed building.

Graffiti can also be an identifying marker. In Northern Ireland, graffiti or murals indicate not only political expression but also religious allegiance and territorial boundaries.

- Read more | From magic spells to dirty graffiti: 16 surprising facts about sex in the classical world

Sometimes, graffiti is poignant. During the First World War, conscientious objectors were held in Richmond Castle in North Yorkshire. Some were forced to fight; others were told that they would be executed for cowardice if they didn’t. One message on the wall, dated 11 August 1916, was written by Percy F Goldsbrough from Pontefract, who shared that he was kept in a cell for “refusing to be made into a soldier”.

For as long as humans exist, so will graffiti. It gives expression to dissent, protest and satire; the simple act of writing a name can in itself also be a political statement. Words will continue to be written in public places, scrubbed out, written again and, sometimes, preserved.

These allow us to hear voices from the past – not those of the great and the good, but of ordinary people.

The graffiti near my home, which I’ve passed every day for 10 years, has become a relic, a familiar part of my existence. Who knows how long it will remain.

This article was first published in the December 2026 issue of HistoryExtra Magazine

Authors

Kavita Puri is a journalist, author and broadcaster. A new edition of her book Partition Voices: Untold British Stories, marking the 75th anniversary of partition, is out now, published by Bloomsbury

item.title: The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

“There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them because it’s sort of obvious.”

Last week, I spoke with Jimmy Wales — the man responsible for Wikipedia, the darling of students all over the world since 2001. Our conversation meandered pleasantly over philosophy, technology, cryptocurrency, politics, history, and more.

But Wales’s fish parable hit me. What “water” do I swim in? Of course, you can take this two ways. First, the water can be seen broadly: the slightly opaque “ways of thinking” we operate under in the 21st-century post-Enlightenment West. We’ll park that discussion for another day. But we can also see this “water” more practically: What specific facts or pieces of information do I think I know, but aren’t as “obvious” as I thought?

I feel as if it’s my philosophical duty to raise doubts where no doubts existed before. And so, here are five “facts” that are actually far more disputed in life — and on Wikipedia — than you might have thought.

1. The Wright brothers invented the airplane

Of course! If you’re feeling really bookish, you could add “Kitty Hawk, December 1903.” The story of the Wright brothers is such a Hollywood-ready fact that it’s almost impossible to forget: two bicycle makers, one windy beach, and twelve seconds in the air.

Unless you went to school in Brazil. Brazilians have two objections to the Wright brothers’ claim: First, no official watched their 1903 flight. Second, the Wright Flyer needed a rail to take off. So, Brazilians give credit for the airplane’s invention to Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew his 14-bis biplane near Paris in the autumn of 1906. He did so in public with Aéro-Club officials on hand to measure it, and he took off on his own wheels.

Wikipedia doesn’t come down on either side. It has a whole article for the rival claims, where the Wrights and Santos-Dumont have to share the page with Gustave Whitehead, Samuel Langley, and a few other men who were absolutely, definitely first.

2. Alan Turing cracked the Enigma code

In 2021, I wrote my book Mini Philosophy, and it was published with three mistakes. First, I wrongly claimed Christopher Nolan directed The Joker. (It was Todd Phillips.) Second, I attributed a quote to Aristotle that actually came from a scholar of Aristotle. But the third mistake, by far and away, was the one that caused the most uproar. I got emails, letters, and pretty intense direct messages. I had claimed the British had cracked the Enigma code. It was Alan Turing and the geniuses of Bletchley Park, surely? That’s what I’d grown up with.

But Enigma was first broken in Warsaw at the end of 1932 by a 27-year-old Polish mathematician named Marian Rejewski. That’s almost seven years before the war began. He and his colleagues, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, spent the 1930s reading German messages. Then, in late July 1939 — five weeks before the invasion of Poland — they invited British and French codebreakers to a forest outside Warsaw and showed them how it was done.

None of this is a secret. Rejewski’s Wikipedia page sums up what he is known for in a single line: “Solving the Enigma machine cipher.” And GCHQ’s own history is happy to say that the first British Bombe owed a great deal to Turing’s meeting with Polish codebreakers. Turing was still a genius, but he was also standing on Polish shoulders.

I mean, really, this fact isn’t so much “disputed” as just “Jonny, you were wrong.”

3. There are seven continents

I kind of knew all the other facts on this list before researching this article, but this one was a shock. Seven. There are seven continents. I admit there’s a bit of controversy around “Australia” vs. “Australasia” vs. “Oceania,” but we all agree on seven, right?

But in Greece and much of the Romance-speaking world, from Lisbon to Lima, children learn that there are six continents, because North and South America are a single continent called “America.” Russian children learn six as well, but a different six: The Americas stay apart, but Europe and Asia are merged into Eurasia. Something a lot of anthropologists and geologists do as well. And the Olympic flag has five rings for five inhabited continents — one America again, with Antarctica left off altogether until the penguins whip together a bobsled team.

The Wikipedia article doesn’t pick a winner. There are, it says, up to seven continents and as few as four. Which means that somewhere, right now, two perfectly well-educated adults are arguing in a pub about something they each learned before they could tie their shoelaces. And they’re both right.

4. The United States won the War of 1812

That depends on who you ask, and in this case, there are three people you could ask.

Ask a Canadian, and you’ll hear about a plucky Canada seeing off an American invasion. Ask an American, and it’s the “Second War of American Independence.” Ask a Brit, and you’ll mostly get a blank look because, for Britain, it was a sideshow to the real business of beating Napoleon. And we’ve loved to hate the French ever since.

In a 2009 poll, 37% of Canadians said Canada won, and only 9% gave it to the United States. Not every American would argue. “By my count,” the American historian Donald Hickey said, “we lost the War of 1812, and we lost Vietnam.”

And Wikipedia? Its editors have spent years on the question. There is a dedicated discussion page titled “Who Won?” and then there was a formal mediation case. And after all that, the article settles on calling the entire debate “inconclusive.”

5. The Second World War began in 1939…

Source: Big Think | Published: 2026-11-25 15:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Flax Seeds of Revolution
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

250 years ago, as the leaves changed and the weather turned colder, General George Washington and the Continental Army marched across Pennsylvania and New Jersey. In the evenings, Washington retreated to his marquee tents, which served as both the center of field command and the general’s private quarters. Through the rain and the ice, Washington camped under a canopy made of linen—trusty, waterproof, and American-made.

In the 1760s, as taxes on British imported goods rose under King George III (r. 1760–1820), American colonists turned to homespun textiles as symbols of resistance and ultimately, independence. One of these textiles was linen, spun and woven from the fibers of the flax plant. Washington’s tent was made by a Pennsylvania upholsterer rather than in private homes, but for women, spinning bees and weaving contests became a way of participating in Revolutionary activities while navigating complex gender dynamics. While cotton is king in the history of American textiles, flax played an important role in the cultural front of the American Revolution, uniting soon-to-be Americans in industriousness and self-sufficiency.

A Brief History of Flax

Flax, or Linum usitatissimum, is one of the oldest continuously cultivated plants in the world, with fibers discovered in the Alps dating back to 5000 BCE. It typically grows in sandy loam and temperate climates, creating blankets of slender stalks and blue flowers in the springtime. Flaxseeds can be ground and eaten or pressed into flaxseed oil or linseed oil. The former is edible and rich in mega-3s, and the latter is used in commodities ranging from paints to linoleum (a material named after the words “linen” and “oil”). But far and away, the most common use of flax is to create the durable, breathable textile—linen.

In ancient Egypt, linen made from flax was ubiquitous, appearing in everything from mummy wrappings to everyday attire. It quickly spread to Europe and beyond. In 789, the future emperor Charlemagne decreed that all households should cultivate their own flax and produce domestic textiles at home.

By the seventeenth century, the weaving of linen was a skilled craft in Europe. Peasants would typically grow, process, and spin their own flax yarn and then bring it to a local artisan—who was usually male—to weave into cloth. As the colonial world expanded, so did the linen trade. Both the Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company had unsuccessfully encouraged settlers at Jamestown and Massachusetts to cultivate flax in the early seventeenth century, but later efforts to grow the crop in North America succeeded. Linen plants were soon growing up and down the East Coast, along with the most productive colonies in the mid-Atlantic region.

The (Flax)seeds of Revolution

In seventeenth-century North America, women spun thread but did not weave; weaving was considered a skilled craft that only a man could hone and monetize. However, by the mid-eighteenth century, the gender norms of linen production were changing. The economy of the thirteen colonies developed rapidly, with complex networks of trade connecting the settlers to mainland England and beyond. Despite the common misconception of early American self-sufficiency, the average colonist spent more than one-quarter of their budget on imports.

Even so, they were no strangers to taxation that caused shockwaves in the homegrown textile economy. The Wool Act of 1699 prevented colonists from exporting their wool to protect the English textile industry. Weaving became a way for daughters to contribute wealth to the household at a time when it was unseemly for them to work in the field or accept wages. As historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich writes, the development of weaving among American women was “neither an artifact of rural poverty nor a response to frontier exigency. It was a colonial adaptation to an expanding mercantile economy.” By the 1770s, the American textile industry was developing rapidly. As such, the act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins.”

Linen was not the only useful flax product in early America. When clothing, tablecloths, and bedsheets wore out, the material was reused for two other essential colonial industries: bookbinding and papermaking. Flax was the material of choice for bookbinding thread due to its durability and strength. Nearly every book printed in the thirteen colonies was stitched with linen thread.

Before paper came to be made by pulping wood, it was crafted from old linen rags. An advertisement in The Massachusetts Spy from October 18, 1779, sought “all Linen & Cotton and Linen Rags, be they ever so small, as they are equally good for the purpose of making paper.” In fact, in 1776, before later transcribing it onto speciallyprepared vellum, the Declaration of Independence was drafted on flax paper. From textile to text, flax bound and dressed the story of America from the very beginning, making the concept of America itself legible for the first time.

Spinning Freedom

For British rule in North America, however, the writing was on the wall as plainly as it would soon be written on the flax. Growing economic dissatisfaction sowed discontent with mainland England. In 1765, the government of King George III passed the Stamp Act, which required written materials such as legal documents and magazines to be printed on London-milled paper embossed with a special stamp. The act enraged the colonial printing industry and papermaking, spurring the slogan “no taxation without representation.” This legislation was soon deemed unenforceable and repealed.…

item.title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.

My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.

Archaeological sites forming in a modern community

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure. Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding, including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes. Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

An ancient city

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials.

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years. Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories.

Climate change at Cahokia

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly. In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes.

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow.” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.

The past and future of climate change

To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “I’m not going to abandon my house. It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding, but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage. I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.

If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost, and some left.…

item.title: Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male-dominated art world by mocking it
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama’s installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the pop art scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the source of her creativity. Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications.

Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world?

Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created Accumulation No. 1, her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical Infinity Mirror Rooms installation.

A major retrospective of her work is on view at the Stedelijk Museum through Jan. 17, 2027.

The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an art historian who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.

Phallic focus

Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the male-dominated New York art world. During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants.

Painter Grace Hartigan had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.

Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond abstract expressionism. The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality coded as masculine. Pop artists refused this model: They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production.

Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show. She decided to focus on sewing — an art rooted in her female Japanese education — and she ordered a sewing machine.

Kusama embraced femininity by using phalluses – a symbol of patriarchal authority – made from assorted fabrics sewn into tubular shapes, filled with cotton and painted white. She upholstered an armchair with these protrusions, colonizing an eerie domestic scene with phalluses made through a traditionally feminine craft.

In this way, she transformed furniture into a vessel of complex meaning, with gender as the key component to interpretation.

Neurosis or intention?

Art critics and scholars have often interpreted the time-consuming process of creating these phalluses as evidence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis. But this assumption overshadows Kusama’s careful planning and deliberate choices in her art. Intensive manual labor is a common component of Kusama’s work.

In 2008, filmmaker Heather Lenz interviewed Kusama’s friend Helen Yrissary, who helped sew the protrusions on the armchair. She noted that while there were always five assistants who crafted the phalluses, only Kusama herself secured them to the chair. In Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, obsession was more of a calculated aesthetic and conceptual choice than a compulsive action.

Kusama knew about obsessive-compulsive disorder and the anxiety it can cause. Drawing on Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories, she explained in her autobiography that she developed the phallic image while she was exploring “kyōfu” – fear, or feelings of the uncanny – in the Accumulation series. According to Freud, the potential for the uncanny is rooted in a child’s first awareness of the anatomical differences between the sexes. He postulated that female children are traumatized when they realize they lack a penis, creating what he called penis envy.

Male authority

Kusama’s Accumulation series may have functioned as a satire of penis envy. And it may have led her to the idea of vanquishing men’s authoritative power.

In one of her self-portraits from 1966, Kusama flaunted a phallic protrusion near her crotch. This gesture suggests that the protrusion might be her own penis, that she might be bisexual or that she might not fall under the category of “female.” Such efforts to redefine female sexuality inspired many female artists at the time. Toward the late 1960s, artist Louise Bourgeois, who admired Kusama’s work, created several sculptures, including Fillette (Little Girl), that employed phallic shapes as commentary on psychological complexes and gender.

But when Kusama premiered Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, The New York Times gave her work only a brief mention. When, three months later, sculptor Claes Oldenburg showed his similarly sewn “metamorphic” sculptures, he received rave reviews in numerous art magazines, bringing him to the attention of the international art world. It was only much later in the 2010s, after Kusama gained global prominence, that Oldenburg admitted her influence on his work.…
